title: Which comparison isolates the core effect?
text:
Choose before opening: compare Trials 1 and 3, or Trials 1 and 4?

Use Trials 1 and 3. Core material changes while turns, core diameter, cells, and wiring stay fixed. Compare both current and clip counts. Trials 1 and 4 change the power source.

title: Does adding turns keep current constant?
text:
Predict: with the same battery, does doubling turns also keep current unchanged?

No. Extra wire increases resistance, so current can fall. Record current as an outcome of the design change. “More turns at the same current” and “more turns on the same battery” are different comparisons.

title: What should you test next?
text:
Your best checked design uses an iron core. To investigate the effect of core diameter, should you also change its cells and turns?

Keep cells, wiring, turns, and core material fixed. Change core diameter, predict the effect, run the test, and check value. Keep the better design as your reference, then investigate another setting. Three designs are a minimum, not a guarantee of reaching 6.38.

title: Can one improved design prove a cause?
text:
A design lifts more clips after both the core and cell arrangement change. Can you conclude that the core alone caused the increase?

No. You found a better combination, but both changes could contribute. Run a matched comparison changing only core material to support a causal explanation.
Make a decision, then check your reasoning

title: Use the right trial pair
html: Core effect: compare Trials 1 and 3. Cell arrangement: compare Trials 4 and 5. For each pair, name the changed setting and controls, then cite current and clip counts. Added turns also add resistance and cost.

title: Search systematically in Trial 6
html:
Record turns, core material, core diameter (mm), cells, wiring, current, clips, cost, wire length, and value ratio. Keep wire at or below 250 cm and cost at or below 50.00.

Predict, change one setting, test, and check both calculations. Keep the best reference design and refine it. Compare at least three distinct checked designs; continue searching until your best ratio rounds to 6.38.

title: Compare value with your baseline
html: Use unrounded ratios from the displayed costs. Round only the final improvement to one decimal place. In your assigned lab, the baseline is your Trial 1 result. The numerical example that follows shows the method using separate fictional records.

title: Worked example: which design gives better value?
html:
Fictional workshop records: A lifts 31 clips for 9.60; B lifts 42 for 12.00; C lifts 40 for 10.40. These invented records teach the calculation and are not outputs to copy into the assigned simulation.

Use A as this example’s baseline. Find the best value and its percentage improvement over A.

title: Calculate the baseline value
html: Divide A’s clips by its displayed cost. Record 3.23 clips per cost unit, but retain the full quotient in your calculator for the percentage calculation.

title: Calculate and compare the other values
html: Calculate each design using its own displayed cost. C has the highest value even though B lifts two more clips. Keep C’s full quotient for the next step.

title: Substitute the unrounded ratios
html: Compare the new ratio with the baseline ratio, not the two clip counts. Enter the original fractions directly so rounding does not accumulate.

title: Round once and interpret the result
html:
The value increased by 19.1%. This describes clips per cost unit, not energy efficiency or just the change in clip count.

If you use the rounded values 3.85 and 3.23 too early, you get 19.2%. Avoid that error by retaining the original fractions.

title: Apply the method to your own checked designs
html:
Keep one complete record per design. Report each ratio to two decimals, compare at least three distinct designs, and calculate your best design’s percentage improvement over your actual Trial 1 baseline.

For the assigned lab, continue until your best checked ratio rounds to 6.38 within the wire and cost limits. This example’s best ratio of 3.85 is only a practice result.

title: Measuring Lifting Performance
text: Record the displayed clips lifted exactly. This is a classroom measure of lifting performance, not a direct magnetic-field measurement in tesla or a guarantee of real hardware performance.

title: Recording Data
text: Prepare one record per trial or design: turns; core material; core diameter (mm); cell count and arrangement; current; clips lifted; displayed cost; wire length; and clips per cost. Note what you changed and why. Keep the original clips and cost for the final percentage calculation. Copy the notes template in the final section to organize your evidence.

text: Next, study a model physical-lab report and a separate three-design comparison. Use their organization to explain your own simulation evidence in the Buzz responses.

Practice designs all meet the limits: A lifts 24 clips for 8.00; B lifts 36 for 12.00; C lifts 35 for 10.00. Using A as the baseline, which design gives the best value and what is its percentage improvement?
C gives 3.50 clips per cost unit, a 16.7% improvement over A.
Correct. A and B each give 3.00 clips per cost unit; C gives 3.50. Use the baseline in the denominator: (3.50 − 3.00) ÷ 3.00 × 100 = 16.7%.
B gives the best value because its clip count is 50% higher than A’s.
B lifts 50% more clips but also costs 50% more. Its value remains 3.00 clips per cost unit, the same as A.
A gives the best value because it has the lowest total cost.
A is cheapest, but C lifts more clips per cost unit: 3.50 compared with 3.00. Compare the ratios, not cost alone.
C gives the best value with a 14.3% improvement over A.
C is the best value, but 14.3% uses the new value as the denominator. Percentage improvement must divide the change by the baseline, 3.00, giving 16.7%.

title: Which axes fit your question?
text: A student changes current and records clips lifted. Which variable belongs on each axis? Put current (A), the changed numerical variable, on the horizontal axis and clips lifted on the vertical axis. Plot the measured values or means and label units. If comparing iron, air, and another core material, use named categories, such as a bar graph, instead of treating materials as numerical values.

title: Does the evidence establish a universal rule?
text: Two tested current levels show a larger mean clip count at the higher current. Does that prove that doubling current always doubles lifting performance? No. State the increase for this tested setup. More current levels and evidence about the model would be needed to justify a wider rule. Clip count is a performance measure, not a direct measurement of magnetic field.

title: Should you discard a result that differs?
text: A physical test gives 9, 10, and 11 clips under the same conditions. Keep all three valid observations and report their mean and spread. Do not remove 9 just to make the result look better. If a documented procedural fault makes a measurement invalid, explain the exclusion and repeat the measurement.

title: What additional evidence would help?
text: For a physical current investigation, test more current levels and repeat each setting to check variation. For the deterministic simulation, test additional distinct designs or a controlled comparison that answers your question. Repeating identical simulation settings does not reveal random measurement uncertainty. Choose a next test that addresses your actual limitation.

title: Annotated model
html:
Claim: “C gave the best value among my three tested designs.”

Numerical evidence: “A, B, and C gave 3.23, 3.50, and 3.85 clips per cost unit. Using the original fractions, C improved value by 19.1% over A.”

Reasoning: “B lifted 42 clips, two more than C, but its greater cost reduced its value. C gave more lifting performance per cost unit.”

Limits and next step: “This comparison identifies the best design I tested, not a universal optimum. Several settings differ, so I cannot attribute the improvement to one cause. I would next vary one setting from C, check both calculations, and continue searching.”

Notice how each sentence has a job. Use the structure with your own checked data; do not copy these invented values.

title: State the question and prediction
html:
Question: How does current affect the number of clips lifted by a fixed coil and core?

Prediction: Raising current from 0.50 A to 1.00 A will increase lifting performance because greater current strengthens the field in the same coil and core. Write the prediction before testing.

title: Show one sample calculation
html:
Add the three observations at each current and divide by three. Then divide the change in the mean by the original mean to find the percentage increase.

Current doubled, but the measured mean clip count increased by 90%, not exactly 100%.
